title: ReAP: From Visual Failure Recognition to Action-Conditioned Risk Prediction for Runtime Failure Monitoring

paper.title: ReAP: From Visual Failure Recognition to Action-Conditioned Risk Prediction for Runtime Failure Monitoring
paper.abstract: Abstract Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle during execution. Reliable deployment therefore requires runtime monitoring that provides timely warnings of failure. Existing monitors commonly estimate risk from current observations or policy signals without explicitly predicting the future consequences of proposed actions. To anticipate such risks before action execution, we introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that combines visual failure recognition with action-conditioned failure prediction. Specifically, ReAP first trains a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn a failure-relevant representation space and estimate current risk. An action-conditioned predictor then forecasts the resulting future representation in this space to estimate future failure risk. At runtime, the detector and predictor provide complementary signals for current-state failure recognition and future-aware risk assessment. Experiments across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world demonstrate that ReAP effectively balances failure-detection accuracy and warning timeliness.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Vision-based monitors estimate failure risk from the current observation, while policy-based monitors rely on signals from the deployed policy. ReAP retains observation-based detection for assessing current risk and augments it with action-conditioned prediction to evaluate the future risk induced by a proposed action before execution. Recent advances in generalist embodied models and policies have substantially expanded the range of manipulation tasks that robots can perform across diverse environments and embodiments ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2026 ) . Despite this progress, learned policies remain vulnerable to unexpected visual changes, imperfect contacts, and compounding action errors, where seemingly small execution deviations can quickly lead to irreversible task failures ( Agia et al., 2025 ) . Runtime failure monitoring is therefore critical for reliable deployment. Timely warnings allow a robot to stop an unsafe action, replan, invoke a fallback strategy, or request human intervention before a recoverable deviation escalates into an irreversible task failure. Existing runtime monitors use different signals to estimate failure risk. Vision-based methods (Figure 1 a ) assess failure from the observed execution state ( Duan et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , while policy-based methods (Figure 1 b ) exploit signals such as policy-internal representations ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ) or uncertainty in the action-generation process ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Rao et al., 2026 ) . These approaches largely assess failure risk from evidence available at the current decision state. However, an execution may still appear nominal even when the proposed action would lead to failure, with the resulting deviation becoming visually apparent only after the action begins. Even from the same state, different actions may steer the execution toward diverse future outcomes, such as recovery or further deviation. Thus, runtime monitoring calls for explicitly looking beyond current evidence and assessing the failure risk of the predicted future state before execution. Motivated by this insight, we introduce ReAP , a future-aware runtime monitoring framework combining visual failure Re cognition with A ction-conditioned risk P rediction. The key idea is to estimate the future failure risk through action-conditioned prediction in a compact visual representation space learned for failure recognition. Specifically, we first train a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn this representation that distinguishes successful and failed observations. Building on this representation, we follow the JEPA-style latent prediction paradigm ( Assran et al., 2023 ) to train an action-conditioned predictor. Given the current visual representation and a proposed action chunk, the predictor models its consequences by estimating the detector representation of the resulting future observation. The frozen detector head is then reused to map this prediction to a future failure-risk score. As illustrated in Figure 1 c , the detector assesses the observed state, whereas the predictor evaluates the proposed action before its outcome becomes observable. We evaluate ReAP across four simulated policy–benchmark settings, covering OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) on LIBERO-10 ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) on eight selected RoboTwin tasks ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . We further deploy the monitor on a real robot across three manipulation tasks using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Across all four simulation settings, our combined monitor consistently outperforms existing baselines, with relative improvements of up to 12.7 % 12.7\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our ReAP in runtime monitoring with low inference overhead. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows: 1. We highlight that many runtime monitors rely only on current execution signals, limiting their ability to predict failures arising from the future consequences of proposed actions. 2. We introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that learns a failure-relevant visual representation and uses action-conditioned latent prediction to estimate the future failure risk associated with proposed actions (Section 4 ). 3. We demonstrate strong monitoring performance across diverse simulated policy–benchmark settings (Section 5.2 ) and real-world manipulation tasks (Section 5.3 ), together with detailed analyses of the detector and predictor components (Section 5.4 ).

sections.heading: Runtime Failure Monitoring
sections.text: Existing runtime failure monitors estimate risk from different execution-time signals. Based on how these signals are processed to assess failure risk, existing approaches can be broadly grouped into four families. OOD-based methods detect deviations from successful or in-distribution behavior ( Burda et al., 2019 ; Wong et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Action-uncertainty methods use signals from generated actions or the action-generation process, including action resampling, diffusion objectives, and flow-matching dynamics ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Rao et al., 2026 ) . Supervised detectors learn failure scores from labeled executions using visual, temporal, or policy representations ( Farid et al., 2022 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . Foundation-model-based approaches use pretrained language or vision-language models for semantic failure detection and reasoning ( Sinha et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2025 ; Pacaud et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Hybrid methods combine multiple signals. FIPER ( Römer et al., 2025 ) combines observation novelty with action uncertainty, while SENTINEL ( Agia et al., 2025 ) combines action uncertainty with VLM-based progress monitoring. A separate line of predictive monitoring models future states under proposed actions. Liu et al. (2024) simulate future policy rollouts with latent dynamics. Concurrent works include Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which uses action-conditioned world-model features for failure detection, and ContactGuard ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which scores predicted post-contact latents with a failure probe. In comparison, ReAP first learns a failure-relevant representation space and models action consequences in this space to estimate future failure risk, considering both current visual signals and future action risks. Further comparisons are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Test-Time Action Evaluation.
sections.text: A growing body of work evaluates candidate actions proposed by robot policies before execution. Recent approaches use learned verifiers, reward models, history-aware verification, or model-internal confidence signals to score and select among multiple action proposals ( Kwok et al., 2025 ; Dai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) . These methods score candidate actions without explicitly predicting their future consequences. A complementary line of work predicts the consequences of candidate actions before evaluation. FOREWARN ( Wu et al., 2025 ) uses a latent world model to imagine candidate outcomes and aligns the predicted latent states with a VLM for consequence evaluation. DynaGuide ( Du and Song, 2025 ) predicts future latent states and uses their similarity to desired or undesired outcomes to guide action generation, while Do What You Say ( Wu et al., 2026 ) forward-simulates candidate action sequences and evaluates whether the predicted outcomes agree with the policy’s textual reasoning. Our method is most closely related to this predictive line, as we use this predictive capability as a runtime monitoring signal by evaluating the estimated representation in the failure-relevant space learned by the visual detector to assess risk before action execution.

sections.heading: 3 Problem Setup
sections.text: We consider runtime failure monitoring for robotic manipulation policies. When queried at environment timestep t t , the deployed policy receives the visual observation O t O_{t} and proposes an action chunk A t π A_{t}^{\pi} of length H π H_{\pi} . The observation-based detector estimates current-state risk r t det r_{t}^{\mathrm{det}} , while the action-conditioned predictor estimates future risk r t + H | t pred r_{t+H|t}^{\mathrm{pred}} associated with executing the first H H actions of A t π A_{t}^{\pi} , denoted by A t = ( a t | t , … , a t + H − 1 | t ) A_{t}=(a_{t|t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1|t}) , where H H is the prediction horizon. Together, they support failure recognition from observed states and anticipation of risky action consequences before execution. The monitoring objective is to detect failed executions as early as possible while limiting false alarms on successful rollouts. Both models are trained on successful and failed rollouts collected from the policy, using only episode-level outcomes. For rollout i i of length T i T_{i} , the risk target is y i , t = 0 y_{i,t}=0 if the rollout succeeds and y i , t = t / ( T i − 1 ) y_{i,t}=t/(T_{i}-1) if it fails, where t ∈ { 0 , … , T i − 1 } t\in\{0,\ldots,T_{i}-1\} . This weak supervision avoids failure-onset annotation and assigns lower risk to early frames that may still appear nominal, with the target increasing to one at the end of a failed rollout. Stage 2 freezes the detector and learns an action-conditioned transition model that predicts future representations, which are evaluated by the same detector head.

sections.heading: 4 Methods
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 , our framework is trained in two stages. In Stage 1, an observation-only failure detector learns a failure-relevant visual representation using episode-level outcome supervision and maps it to a scalar risk score. In Stage 2, an action-conditioned transition model is trained in the latent space learned in Stage 1 to predict how the detector representation changes after executing a candidate action chunk. The predicted future representation is evaluated by the same frozen detector head, keeping the risk semantics of observed and predicted representations fixed. After training, thresholds for the detector and predictor are calibrated separately on held-out successful rollouts.

sections.heading: 4.1 Observation-Only Failure Representation Learning
sections.text: Stage 1 learns a policy-external representation of failure from the current visual observation O t O_{t} , without accessing candidate actions or internal policy features. Each observation may contain one or more synchronized camera views. For each camera view, dense patch tokens are extracted using a frozen DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) backbone. The tokens are projected into a shared feature space and augmented with camera-specific and spatial positional embeddings. Tokens from all views are then concatenated to form the visual tokens of O t O_{t} . To compress the dense visual features into a failure-relevant representation, we use a Perceiver-style feature extractor ( Jaegle et al., 2021 ) with a fixed set of M M learnable latent queries. The latent queries aggregate visual information through cross-attention, using the projected DINOv2 patch tokens as keys and values. This produces a fixed set of M M detector latent tokens, denoted by L t L_{t} . We use M = 32 M=32 in all experiments. The detector latent tokens are first mean-pooled into a single vector that summarizes the current observation. A learned linear projection then maps this vector to the compact state representation z t z_{t} . Finally, the detector head maps z t z_{t} to the observation-level risk score r t det ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}\in[0,1] . During Stage 1 training, the DINOv2 backbone remains frozen, while the visual projection, Perceiver-style feature extractor, and detector head are optimized using failure supervision. To train the detector, we use a class-weighted binary cross-entropy loss over valid observation timesteps: ℒ det = − ∑ i ∑ t [ w + y i , t log r i , t det + w − ( 1 − y i , t ) log ( 1 − r i , t det ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=-\sum_{i}\sum_{t}\left[w_{+}y_{i,t}\log r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{det}}+w_{-}(1-y_{i,t})\log(1-r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{det}})\right], (1) where y i , t y_{i,t} is the risk target defined in Section 3 , and w + w_{+} and w − w_{-} compensate for class imbalance.

sections.heading: 4.2 Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics in Failure Space
sections.text: Stage 2 models how a candidate action chunk changes the failure-relevant representation learned in Stage 1. Inspired by JEPA-style latent prediction ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) , we predict the representation of the future observation directly in the learned latent space rather than reconstructing the observation itself. The complete Stage 1 detector is frozen throughout this stage. Given the current compact representation z t z_{t} and the action proposal A t A_{t} available from the current policy query, each action is independently projected to the transition latent dimension and augmented with a learnable step embedding that encodes its position within the action chunk. The resulting action tokens serve as queries in stacked cross-attention blocks. To construct the keys and values, we apply linear projections independently to each token in L t L_{t} . The cross-attention blocks attend to these projected tokens and produce action-conditioned features over the prediction horizon. We mean-pool both the action tokens and the resulting action-conditioned features, and concatenate them with the current compact representation z t z_{t} . A residual transition MLP takes the concatenated features as input and predicts a latent update, which is added to the current representation z t z_{t} to obtain the future compact representation z ^ t + H | t \hat{z}_{t+H|t} . sections.heading: 4.3 Threshold Calibration
sections.text: Following prior work on time-dependent failure-score calibration ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , we calibrate monitoring thresholds using a held-out set of successful rollouts. Scores estimated may vary across execution phases even in successful rollouts, motivating thresholds that vary with time. To align score trajectories for calibration, we consider three temporal parameterizations. Absolute-time calibration indexes thresholds by the raw timestep t t . Normalized-time calibration represents each timestep by its relative progress within the trajectory. Staged-time calibration partitions normalized execution progress into a fixed number of stages and uses a shared threshold within each stage. For each temporal parameterization, we construct thresholds using either pointwise quantiles or a one-sided functional conformal band, resulting in six calibration variants. The detector and predictor are calibrated independently under the same protocol. For further details, refer to Appendix E . Let δ t det \delta_{t}^{\mathrm{det}} and δ t pred \delta_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}} denote their respective thresholds. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate ReAP in simulation and on real robots to answer three questions. (1) Does ReAP achieve a favorable balance between failure-detection accuracy, warning timeliness, and false alarms across diverse policies and tasks? (Section 5.2 and Appendix D.1 ) (2) Can ReAP maintain effective online monitoring on real robots while introducing low inference overhead? (Section 5.3 ) (3) What enables its monitoring performance, and how do failure-relevant representation learning and action-conditioned prediction contribute to the final monitor? (Section 5.4 and Appendix D.2 )

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare ReAP with representative runtime failure monitors from three categories. Action-uncertainty methods estimate failure risk from the policy’s action-generation process. STAC ( Agia et al., 2025 ) measures inconsistency across sampled actions, Diff-DAgger ( Lee et al., 2025 ) uses diffusion-model objectives as uncertainty signals, and ACCEL ( Rao et al., 2026 ) derives uncertainty from flow-matching trajectories. OOD-based methods identify failures from deviations relative to successful execution. We include RND ( Burda et al., 2019 ) and LogpZO ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , and additionally evaluate FIPER ( Römer et al., 2025 ) , which augments an observation-based OOD signal with action uncertainty. Classifier-based methods directly learn failure risk from successful and failed rollouts. We include SAFE-MLP and SAFE-LSTM ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , which operate on internal VLA representations extracted from the deployed policy.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocols.
sections.text: Following Römer et al. (2025) , we evaluate runtime monitoring with three complementary metrics, balanced time-weighted accuracy (bTWA), balanced accuracy (bACC), and normalized detection time (T-det). bACC measures failure-detection accuracy while accounting for false alarms on successful rollouts, with bACC = ( TPR + TNR ) / 2 \mathrm{bACC}=(\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2 . T-det measures warning timeliness as the mean normalized first-alarm time over all failed rollouts, with missed failures assigned a value of one. We use bTWA as the primary metric because it jointly rewards failure detection and early warning while penalizing missed failures and false alarms: bTWA = 1 2 ​ ( 1 N fail ​ ∑ i ∈ TP ( 1 − t i T i ) + N TN N succ ) , \mathrm{bTWA}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{fail}}}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{TP}}\left(1-\frac{t_{i}}{T_{i}}\right)+\frac{N_{\mathrm{TN}}}{N_{\mathrm{succ}}}\right), (4) Here, TP \mathrm{TP} denotes the set of failed rollouts that are detected, and t i t_{i} and T i T_{i} denote the first-alarm time and rollout length for a correctly detected failure. sections.heading: Results Analysis.
sections.text: Table 1 shows that ReAP achieves the highest bTWA across all four policy–benchmark settings, with relative improvements of up to 12.7 % 12.7\% over the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting. Averaged across the four settings, ReAP achieves a bTWA of 0.708 0.708 , a bACC of 0.800 0.800 , and a T-det of 0.405 0.405 . These results demonstrate a favorable balance between failure-detection accuracy and warning timeliness across different policy architectures and manipulation benchmarks. The baseline results reveal different limitations in achieving this balance between accuracy and timeliness. Action-uncertainty methods can produce early warnings but often with lower balanced accuracy. For example, Diff-DAgger reaches a T-det of 0.163 0.163 on π 0 \pi_{0} /LIBERO-10, while its bACC is only 0.531 0.531 . In contrast, OOD-based methods often achieve stronger balanced accuracy but raise alarms later. FIPER obtains a bACC of 0.808 0.808 on OpenVLA/LIBERO-10, but with a T-det of 0.812 0.812 . SAFE is competitive in several settings, yet its performance varies across policies. To assess how the two branches contribute to these gains, we also report the results of the detector and predictor. Both branches of ReAP already provide strong standalone monitoring signals. The detector effectively recognizes failure evidence from observed execution states, while the predictor achieves comparable or stronger performance through action-conditioned consequence prediction. Applying the OR rule further improves bTWA over both components in all four settings and consistently reduces normalized detection time. These consistent gains support the complementary roles of current-state failure recognition and action-conditioned future-risk prediction.

sections.heading: Architecture Ablation.
sections.text: We ablate the feature extractor and latent-token aggregation in the observation-only detector. The Raw DINOv2 baseline directly mean-pools frozen DINOv2 patch features without the Perceiver-style feature extractor. The remaining variants use the Perceiver-style extractor to produce a fixed set of latent tokens and differ only in how these tokens are aggregated, using an MLP, self-attention, or mean pooling. As shown in Figure 3(a) , directly mean-pooling frozen DINOv2 features already achieves a bTWA of 0.635 0.635 , exceeding the strongest baseline in the main benchmark at 0.622 0.622 . Introducing the failure-supervised feature extractor further improves bTWA to 0.671 0.671 with mean pooling, supporting the benefit of learning monitoring-relevant features on top of the frozen visual backbone. Mean pooling performs best among the aggregation variants, and we adopt it together with the learned feature extractor in the default detector.

sections.heading: Representation Structure.
sections.text: To examine how failure supervision separates successful and failed observations, we compare the learned detector representation with frozen DINOv2 patch features and OpenVLA internal representations in Figure 4 . In the 2D PCA projection, DINOv2 features are organized primarily by task appearance, with successful and failed observations from the same task remaining close to each other. OpenVLA features similarly show limited separation by execution outcome. In contrast, the learned detector representation forms a more coherent failure region shared across tasks, with late-stage observations from failed rollouts clustering more closely in the projected space. Together with the quantitative gains in Figure 3(a) , this suggests that the learned representation captures failure-related structure shared across the evaluated tasks.

sections.heading: Prediction Representation.
sections.text: Beyond the training objective, we assess how the representation space affects future-risk prediction by comparing three variants with the Stage 2 predictor architecture fixed. Generic PCA compresses frozen DINOv2 features using PCA, Random detector uses the same detector architecture without failure supervision, and Learned detector uses the representation obtained after Stage 1 training. For the first two variants, the corresponding detector head is learned jointly with the predictor. As shown in Table 3 a , predicting in the learned detector space achieves the strongest performance, reaching a bTWA of 0.683 0.683 and a bACC of 0.764 0.764 , compared with 0.650 0.650 and 0.752 0.752 for the random detector and 0.644 0.644 and 0.747 0.747 for Generic PCA. Adding the latent-transition loss to the random-detector variant yields only a small increase in mean bTWA. Together with the stronger performance of the learned detector, this suggests that failure-supervised detector features provide more effective prediction targets for future-risk estimation than generic or randomly initialized representations.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented ReAP, a future-aware runtime failure monitoring framework that builds on visual failure recognition to predict future action risks. A visual detector learns a failure-relevant representation space from successful and failed rollouts, within which an action-conditioned predictor estimates future representations and their associated risk. The combined monitor achieves the highest bTWA across all four simulated policy–benchmark settings, supporting the complementary value of current-state recognition and future-risk prediction in balancing failure detection, warning timeliness, and false alarms. Real-robot experiments demonstrate effective online monitoring, and runtime measurements indicate limited inference overhead. Component analyses further support the roles of failure-supervised representation learning and action conditioning in improving future-latent prediction and failure-risk estimation.

sections.heading: Appendix A Comparison with Model-Based Predictive Monitors
sections.text: Liu et al. (2024) combine latent-dynamics prediction, OOD detection, and learned failure classification within interactive imitation learning, using human intervention states to supervise failure detection. Their follow-up work, Sirius-Fleet ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , extends predictive monitoring to multi-task robot fleets, using visual world models and anomaly predictors to guide human intervention. Concurrent works, Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) and ContactGuard ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , also assess the anticipated consequences of proposed actions. Below, we clarify how ReAP relates to these approaches.

sections.heading: Failure supervision and prediction space.
sections.text: Foresight freezes a video-pretrained V-JEPA 2 encoder ( Assran et al., 2025 ) and learns an action-conditioned predictor before training a downstream failure detector. ContactGuard learns a JEPA-style world model from unlabelled robot trajectories, then freezes it and fits a linear failure probe. In ReAP, failure supervision first shapes a compact representation on top of a frozen visual backbone. We then freeze the detector and learn action-conditioned transitions within this representation space, using both latent-transition and future-risk supervision. The same frozen detector head scores observed and predicted representations. Thus, failure supervision determines the target space for prediction as well as the subsequent risk readout.

sections.heading: Monitoring scope and temporal context.
sections.text: Foresight aggregates predicted-latent tokens from the execution history with a causal Transformer and uses trajectory-level outcome labels. ContactGuard uses labelled grasp clips and a gripper-closure trigger to assess predicted post-contact states before contact occurs. ReAP also learns from episode-level outcomes, while combining current-observation and predicted-state alarms throughout execution. Its observation branch can assess incoming images independently of action generation, and its prediction branch evaluates proposed action chunks. This design requires neither a contact-event trigger nor a temporal aggregation head.

sections.heading: Runtime considerations.
sections.text: Foresight reports 183.64 183.64 ms per monitoring call with its Transformer head on an NVIDIA H200 GPU ( Zhang et al., 2026 , Table 14) . ContactGuard reports 19.18 19.18 ms for encoding, a 30-step latent rollout, and classification on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 ( Zheng et al., 2026 , Table 4) . Both reported latencies exclude policy inference. In our setup, the detector takes 9.72 9.72 ms, while predictor-based monitoring takes 81.16 81.16 ms including policy inference on an NVIDIA A800 80GB GPU (Table 2 b ). Differences in hardware, prediction horizons, and timing boundaries prevent a controlled speed comparison. Our measurements support the practicality of a fast observation branch that can issue alarms without waiting for policy inference.

sections.heading: Implications for generalization.
sections.text: Foresight’s video pretraining may provide temporal and physical priors that help transfer to new settings. Our representation learns failure-related cues from labeled rollouts, so its transfer performance may depend on the range of tasks and failure modes covered during training. Evaluating both approaches under the same task and policy shifts would help establish how these differences affect their generalization.

sections.heading: Appendix B Comparison with Vision-Based Monitors
sections.text: Several recent failure monitors assess robot execution directly from visual observations or visually grounded representations. VLM-based approaches exploit semantic reasoning to recognize and interpret manipulation failures. AHA ( Duan et al., 2025 ) formulates failure detection as free-form visual reasoning, while Guardian ( Pacaud et al., 2025 ) learns detailed failure detection and reasoning from automatically synthesized failure data. FailSafe ( Lin et al., 2025 ) extends visual failure reasoning toward recovery, and ViFailback ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) uses real-world failure trajectories to train a VLM for failure diagnosis and visually grounded correction guidance. SENTINEL ( Agia et al., 2025 ) incorporates a VLM-based progress monitor alongside a separate action-consistency signal for runtime failure detection. More broadly, recent progress and reward models learn from large-scale robot trajectory datasets to assess task progress and execution quality across successful and unsuccessful rollouts ( Liang et al., 2026 ; ACE-Brain Team et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . RC-NF ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , for example, combines object-motion cues extracted from visual observations with robot state in a robot-conditioned normalizing flow for real-time anomaly detection. Many existing vision-based monitors rely on multi-billion-parameter vision-language models, and some additionally require explicit semantic reasoning, leading to substantially higher computational cost than lightweight per-step monitors. This observation is consistent with recent VLM-critic work showing that distinguishing fine-grained visual differences between successful and failed executions remains challenging for vision-language models ( Sudhakar et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: C.2 Baseline Implementations
sections.text: For RND, LogpZO, SAFE-MLP, and SAFE-LSTM, we build on the public SAFE implementation 1 1 1 https://github.com/vla-safe/SAFE and follow its model architectures and optimization hyperparameters unless otherwise specified. RND and LogpZO are trained only on successful rollouts and therefore do not use failure-risk labels. For the supervised SAFE baselines, we replace the binary failure target with the same temporally increasing target y t = t / ( T − 1 ) y_{t}=t/(T-1) used by our detector as discussed above. For baselines that operate on policy representations, we follow SAFE for feature extraction whenever applicable. For OpenVLA, we mean-pool the hidden states corresponding to the seven autoregressive action tokens, yielding a 4096-D representation. For π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we average action-expert suffix hidden states across the action horizon and ten flow-matching steps to obtain a 1024-D representation. For Fast-WAM, we mean-pool the final video-MoT policy tokens into a 3072-D representation. STAC, Diff-DAgger, ACCEL, and FIPER are implemented following their respective public implementations. For methods that require repeated action sampling, we generate 32 action chunks at each replanning step. We retain the sampled action chunks and intermediate flow trajectories required by the corresponding baselines. For Fast-WAM, repeated-sampling methods likewise use 32 action samples with an action horizon of 32 and ten inference steps. OpenVLA requires separate treatment because its standard rollout policy uses deterministic autoregressive decoding. We apply this sampling procedure only to FIPER, whose action-uncertainty component can be constructed directly from a set of stochastic action proposals. Diff-DAgger and ACCEL require policy-specific diffusion or flow-matching quantities that are not defined for OpenVLA. STAC is not applicable to OpenVLA because it requires temporally overlapping action chunks across consecutive policy queries, whereas OpenVLA predicts only a single immediate action per query. We evaluate FIPER on OpenVLA using stochastic action proposals following the sampling strategy of RoboMonkey ( Kwok et al., 2025 ) . Specifically, we first obtain multiple valid action samples through stochastic autoregressive decoding, then fit a diagonal Gaussian to the first six continuous action dimensions, and draw additional proposals from the fitted distribution. The gripper action is determined by majority vote, and continuous actions are clipped to the policy action-statistics range. This sampling procedure is used only to construct the FIPER uncertainty signal and does not alter the deterministic OpenVLA rollouts used for evaluation. FIPER uses the thresholding procedure from its original implementation. For the remaining baselines, we select the time-varying calibration variant using the validation split and fit its thresholds on the held-out successful calibration rollouts using our six calibration variants.

sections.heading: C.4 Real-Robot Setup
sections.text: Our real-world experiments use a dual-arm robotic platform consisting of two AgileX PIPER manipulators. Visual observations are captured by three Intel RealSense D435i cameras, including one global third-person camera and one wrist-mounted camera on each arm. For each manipulation task, we deploy a separately fine-tuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy and train a task-specific ReAP monitor using the same model architecture and training configuration as in simulation. Our deployment system is built on the Evo-RL framework ( Evo-RL Contributors, 2026 ) , which we extend to support runtime failure monitoring. Observation acquisition, policy inference, and robot control run in separate processes. A dedicated observation server continuously provides the latest synchronized camera observations. The control process retrieves the latest observation and sends it to a remote inference server, where the deployed policy generates the next action chunk. The predictor runs alongside the policy on the inference server and evaluates each proposed action chunk before execution, while the observation-based detector runs independently on a local NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU and monitors incoming observations without waiting for policy inference. The action chunk returned by the server is then executed by the robot. Whenever either branch raises an alarm, we record the alarm together with the corresponding rollout information for subsequent evaluation. ReAP is the only monitor integrated into the live deployment system. Baseline predictions are generated post hoc from the same recorded observations and policy outputs. Since monitoring alarms do not alter robot execution, all methods are evaluated on identical successful and failed trajectories, enabling paired comparison without collecting separate physical rollouts for each baseline. sections.heading: Seen-to-unseen generalization.
sections.text: A useful failure representation should preserve failure-relevant cues as task appearance and interaction context change ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . We evaluate this property on OpenVLA by randomly selecting three LIBERO-10 tasks (Task 1, 4, 7) as unseen tasks, training all methods on the remaining seen tasks, calibrating corresponding thresholds on unseen tasks, and evaluating them on a disjoint set of unseen-task rollouts without further model training. As shown in Table 10 , performance on unseen tasks is relatively close across methods, reflecting the difficulty of transferring failure-monitoring signals across task distributions. ReAP achieves the highest mean performance, reaching 0.568 bTWA and 0.677 bACC. This suggests that the failure-supervised representation captures failure cues that remain useful beyond the tasks observed during training. However, the margin over the strongest baselines is modest, indicating that cross-task transfer remains challenging and that the learned failure representation is still affected by task-specific visual and interaction patterns. sections.heading: Cross-policy generalization.
sections.text: We next evaluate whether ReAP transfers across policies on LIBERO-10. Since ReAP relies on external visual observations and proposed action chunks without accessing policy-internal representations, the same monitor can be applied to a different policy without architectural modification. We train and calibrate the monitor using rollouts from one source policy and directly evaluate it on another target policy without additional adaptation. For each transfer direction, we train the monitor on source-policy rollouts using the prediction horizon available at target-policy evaluation. For OpenVLA → π 0 \rightarrow\pi_{0} , we construct ten-step action sequences from consecutive actions in the recorded OpenVLA rollouts and train the predictor with H = 10 H=10 . At evaluation, we use the first ten actions of each action chunk proposed by π 0 \pi_{0} . For π 0 → \pi_{0}\rightarrow OpenVLA, we train and evaluate with H = 1 H=1 , matching OpenVLA’s single-step action proposal. As shown in Table 10 , OpenVLA → π 0 \rightarrow\pi_{0} achieves 0.746 bTWA, compared with 0.780 under π 0 \pi_{0} in-policy training in Table 1 , while π 0 → \pi_{0}\rightarrow OpenVLA reaches 0.629 compared with 0.701 under the corresponding OpenVLA in-policy setting. Although performance decreases after transferring across policies, it remains relatively close to the corresponding in-policy results in both settings. This shows that ReAP can preserve useful failure-monitoring capability across different deployed policies without target-policy adaptation. We further compare cross-policy transfer with RoboMeter, since it is likewise independent of policy-internal signals. When transferring to π 0 \pi_{0} , ReAP achieves 0.746 bTWA and 0.818 bACC, compared with 0.685 and 0.786 for RoboMeter. When transferring to OpenVLA, the two methods perform comparably, with ReAP obtaining 0.629 bTWA and 0.676 bACC and RoboMeter obtaining 0.630 and 0.685. Across the two transfer settings, ReAP therefore maintains a relatively stable advantage or comparable performance against RoboMeter.

sections.heading: D.3 Alarm Timing Relative to Annotated Failure Onset
sections.text: To provide a temporal reference for evaluating alarm timing, we use Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) to obtain approximate failure-onset annotations for failed rollouts on LIBERO-10. We adapt the annotation prompt from Appendix F.1 of Park et al. (2026) and use a coarse-to-fine procedure with two successive model calls per rollout. In both calls, the model receives image grids containing the main-camera and wrist-camera views at each sampled time point, labeled with the frame index and timestamp. The first call locates the approximate onset using frames sampled throughout the rollout every 25 timesteps, including the first and last frames. Each 535-frame failed rollout yields 23 sampled time points, arranged into four image grids. As described in Appendix E , pointwise calibration estimates a separate quantile at each temporal position. However, a successful rollout is counted as a false alarm if its score crosses the threshold at any monitored timestep, so controlling exceedances separately at each position does not directly control false alarms over the full rollout. sections.heading: Appendix E Time-Varying Threshold Calibration
sections.text: We calibrate alarm thresholds using held-out successful rollouts to account for variation in risk scores over the course of execution. For rollout i i , let T i T_{i} denote its full length in environment frames. A monitoring branch records L i L_{i} risk scores, forming the sequence 𝐬 i = ( s i , 0 , … , s i , L i − 1 ) \mathbf{s}_{i}=(s_{i,0},\ldots,s_{i,L_{i}-1}) . Each score s i , j s_{i,j} is associated with an original frame index f i , j f_{i,j} , and larger scores indicate higher predicted failure risk. For the predictor, f i , j f_{i,j} refers to the decision frame at which the proposed action chunk is evaluated. We calibrate thresholds separately for the detector and predictor. For each branch, let 𝒟 cal = { 𝐬 1 , … , 𝐬 N } \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{\mathbf{s}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{s}_{N}\} denote the risk-score sequences from held-out successful rollouts. These sequences are used to estimate a time-varying upper threshold δ j ​ ( α ) \delta_{j}(\alpha) , where j j indexes monitored positions under the chosen temporal parameterization. We evaluate α ∈ { 0.05 , 0.10 , 0.15 , 0.20 , 0.25 } \alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25\} and use the same α \alpha for both branches. Each branch raises an alarm at the first position satisfying s i , j ≥ δ j ​ ( α ) s_{i,j}\geq\delta_{j}(\alpha) , and the two branches’ alarms are combined using the OR rule described in the main paper. A single global threshold ignores temporal variation in the score distribution over the course of an execution. Successful manipulation trajectories can exhibit different nominal risk levels during phases such as free-space motion, contact, grasping, and placement. We therefore consider three temporal parameterizations consisting of normalized time, absolute time, and fixed execution stages. Each temporal parameterization is paired with either pointwise empirical-quantile calibration or functional conformal calibration, resulting in the six variants illustrated in Figure 8 . Figure 8: Illustration of the six time-varying threshold calibration variants. The top row shows pointwise empirical-quantile calibration and the bottom row shows functional calibration. From left to right, the columns use absolute time, normalized execution progress, and fixed execution stages. Thin gray curves denote successful calibration trajectories. Dark curves in the top row indicate thresholds at representative significance levels α \alpha , while the bottom row shows the nominal trajectory together with the corresponding functional upper bands. Smaller α \alpha produces a more conservative upper boundary.

sections.heading: Absolute time.
sections.text: Absolute-time calibration aligns successful trajectories by their monitored score index j j . Let L max = max i ⁡ L i L_{\max}=\max_{i}L_{i} be the maximum number of recorded scores among successful calibration trajectories. Shorter score sequences are extended to L max L_{\max} by repeating their final score. Thresholds are then constructed as a function of the absolute score index. This parameterization can be applied online using only the current timestep and does not require knowing the final duration of the test rollout. However, when rollout lengths vary, the same absolute timestep may correspond to different stages of task execution across trajectories. If a test rollout contains more than L max L_{\max} recorded scores, the final calibrated threshold is used for all subsequent positions.

sections.heading: Normalized time.
sections.text: Normalized-time calibration aligns trajectories according to relative execution progress rather than absolute timestep. For calibration rollout i i , we define normalized progress as u i , t = t T i − 1 , u_{i,t}=\frac{t}{T_{i}-1}, and linearly interpolate its risk trajectory onto a common grid of G G normalized positions between 0 and 1. We use G = 100 G=100 in all experiments. This representation removes differences in raw rollout duration during calibration and aligns trajectories according to their relative progress. At deployment, the final duration of an ongoing rollout is unavailable. We therefore define a reference rollout length T ref = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N T i T_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_{i} using only successful calibration rollouts. The current timestep is mapped to normalized progress using T ref T_{\mathrm{ref}} and then to the corresponding position on the calibrated grid. If execution exceeds T ref T_{\mathrm{ref}} , the threshold at the final normalized position is retained. In this way, no information about the final duration of the test rollout is used.

sections.heading: Staged time.
sections.text: Staged-time calibration provides a coarser representation of relative execution progress. Each successful calibration trajectory is divided into K K equally spaced stages according to normalized time, and all risk scores within the same stage share one threshold. We use K = 10 K=10 in all experiments. This produces a piecewise-constant threshold trajectory while preserving the coarse progression of risk over an execution. For pointwise calibration, successful scores assigned to the same stage are pooled when estimating that stage’s upper quantile. For functional calibration, we instead take the maximum score within each stage of each successful rollout. This yields one K K -dimensional stage-level trajectory per rollout, to which the functional-band procedure is applied. At deployment, the current timestep is mapped to a stage using the same reference rollout length T ref T_{\mathrm{ref}} . If execution extends beyond T ref T_{\mathrm{ref}} , the threshold of the final stage is retained.

sections.heading: E.2 Pointwise Empirical Quantile Calibration
sections.text: For normalized-time and absolute-time parameterizations, pointwise calibration estimates an upper empirical quantile independently at each aligned temporal position. Let s ~ i , j \widetilde{s}_{i,j} denote the aligned score of calibration rollout i i at temporal position j j . The threshold is δ j ​ ( α ) = Q 1 − α ​ ( s ~ 1 , j , … , s ~ N , j ) , \delta_{j}(\alpha)=Q_{1-\alpha}\left(\widetilde{s}_{1,j},\ldots,\widetilde{s}_{N,j}\right), (6) where Q 1 − α Q_{1-\alpha} denotes the empirical ( 1 − α ) (1-\alpha) -quantile. For the staged-time parameterization, the same construction is applied to all successful scores assigned to each stage. Pointwise calibration follows local changes in the nominal score distribution, but different temporal positions are calibrated independently. A pointwise significance level therefore does not imply that an entire successful trajectory remains below the threshold simultaneously. We use empirical upper quantiles directly and interpret α \alpha as the significance level indexing the resulting operating point.

sections.heading: E.3 Functional Conformal Calibration
sections.text: Conformal prediction provides a distribution-free framework for calibration under exchangeability ( Vovk et al., 2005 ; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023 ) . Functional conformal prediction extends this construction to function-valued observations and simultaneous prediction bands ( Diquigiovanni et al., 2022 ; Diquigiovanni et al., 2025 ) . Trajectory-level calibration has also been adopted in recent runtime failure monitoring methods ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In our setting, an entire successful risk trajectory is treated as one functional observation. For each temporal parameterization, the calibration set is divided into two disjoint subsets, 𝒟 A \mathcal{D}_{A} and 𝒟 B \mathcal{D}_{B} . The first estimates the nominal trajectory and its temporal variation, while the second calibrates the width of the upper band. sections.heading: E.4 Independent Calibration and OR Fusion
sections.text: The significance level α \alpha controls the sensitivity of each calibrated monitoring branch. A smaller α \alpha generally produces a higher and more conservative threshold, which tends to reduce false alarms but may delay or miss failures. A larger α \alpha lowers the threshold and increases sensitivity, typically yielding earlier alarms at the cost of more false positives. Previous calibration-based monitors typically associate α \alpha with the monitoring score that directly determines the final alarm ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . For example, SAFE ( Gu et al., 2025 ) uses functional conformal prediction to bound the probability of raising any alarm during a successful rollout by α \alpha , under the exchangeability assumption. In ReAP, the detector and predictor are calibrated separately at the same α \alpha , and their alarms are combined using an OR rule. A branch-level guarantee therefore does not directly imply the same guarantee for the combined monitor. Let A det A_{\mathrm{det}} and A pred A_{\mathrm{pred}} denote the events that the respective branches raise an alarm on a successful rollout. If each branch satisfies Pr ⁡ ( A det ) ≤ α \Pr(A_{\mathrm{det}})\leq\alpha and Pr ⁡ ( A pred ) ≤ α \Pr(A_{\mathrm{pred}})\leq\alpha , the union bound gives Pr ⁡ ( A det ∪ A pred ) ≤ Pr ⁡ ( A det ) + Pr ⁡ ( A pred ) ≤ 2 ​ α . \Pr(A_{\mathrm{det}}\cup A_{\mathrm{pred}})\leq\Pr(A_{\mathrm{det}})+\Pr(A_{\mathrm{pred}})\leq 2\alpha. This bound does not require independence between the two branches. It describes how branch-level false-alarm guarantees would translate under OR fusion. In our implementation, α \alpha serves as a nominal branch-level calibration parameter, and the false-alarm rate of the combined monitor is evaluated empirically on the held-out evaluation split.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.16309v1 [cs.RO] 12 Oct 2026 ReAP: From Visual Failure Recognition to Action-Conditioned Risk Prediction for Runtime Failure Monitoring Jingyuan Liu † † thanks: Email: 23302010010@m.fudan.edu.cn Affiliation: ACE Robotics Affiliation: Fudan University Yunpeng Qing Affiliation: ACE Robotics Affiliation: Zhejiang University Changxu Wei Affiliation: ACE Robotics Affiliation: PolyU Zhi Hou Affiliation: ACE Robotics Abstract Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle during execution. Reliable deployment therefore requires runtime monitoring that provides timely warnings of failure. Existing monitors commonly estimate risk from current observations or policy signals without explicitly predicting the future consequences of proposed actions. To anticipate such risks before action execution, we introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that combines visual failure recognition with action-conditioned failure prediction. Specifically, ReAP first trains a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn a failure-relevant representation space and estimate current risk. An action-conditioned predictor then forecasts the resulting future representation in this space to estimate future failure risk. At runtime, the detector and predictor provide complementary signals for current-state failure recognition and future-aware risk assessment. Experiments across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world demonstrate that ReAP effectively balances failure-detection accuracy and warning timeliness. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Vision-based monitors estimate failure risk from the current observation, while policy-based monitors rely on signals from the deployed policy. ReAP retains observation-based detection for assessing current risk and augments it with action-conditioned prediction to evaluate the future risk induced by a proposed action before execution. Recent advances in generalist embodied models and policies have substantially expanded the range of manipulation tasks that robots can perform across diverse environments and embodiments ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2026 ) . Despite this progress, learned policies remain vulnerable to unexpected visual changes, imperfect contacts, and compounding action errors, where seemingly small execution deviations can quickly lead to irreversible task failures ( Agia et al., 2025 ) . Runtime failure monitoring is therefore critical for reliable deployment. Timely warnings allow a robot to stop an unsafe action, replan, invoke a fallback strategy, or request human intervention before a recoverable deviation escalates into an irreversible task failure. Existing runtime monitors use different signals to estimate failure risk. Vision-based methods (Figure 1 a ) assess failure from the observed execution state ( Duan et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , while policy-based methods (Figure 1 b ) exploit signals such as policy-internal representations ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ) or uncertainty in the action-generation process ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Rao et al., 2026 ) . These approaches largely assess failure risk from evidence available at the current decision state. However, an execution may still appear nominal even when the proposed action would lead to failure, with the resulting deviation becoming visually apparent only after the action begins. Even from the same state, different actions may steer the execution toward diverse future outcomes, such as recovery or further deviation. Thus, runtime monitoring calls for explicitly looking beyond current evidence and assessing the failure risk of the predicted future state before execution. Motivated by this insight, we introduce ReAP , a future-aware runtime monitoring framework combining visual failure Re cognition with A ction-conditioned risk P rediction. The key idea is to estimate the future failure risk through action-conditioned prediction in a compact visual representation space learned for failure recognition. Specifically, we first train a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn this representation that distinguishes successful and failed observations. Building on this representation, we follow the JEPA-style latent prediction paradigm ( Assran et al., 2023 ) to train an action-conditioned predictor. Given the current visual representation and a proposed action chunk, the predictor models its consequences by estimating the detector representation of the resulting future observation. The frozen detector head is then reused to map this prediction to a future failure-risk score. As illustrated in Figure 1 c , the detector assesses the observed state, whereas the predictor evaluates the proposed action before its outcome becomes observable. We evaluate ReAP across four simulated policy–benchmark settings, covering OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) on LIBERO-10 ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) on eight selected RoboTwin tasks ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . We further deploy the monitor on a real robot across three manipulation tasks using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Across all four simulation settings, our combined monitor consistently outperforms existing baselines, with relative improvements of up to 12.7 % 12.7\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our ReAP in runtime monitoring with low inference overhead. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows: 1. We highlight that many runtime monitors rely only on current execution signals, limiting their ability to predict failures arising from the future consequences of proposed actions. 2. We introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that learns a failure-relevant visual representation and uses action-conditioned latent prediction to estimate the future failure risk associated with proposed actions (Section 4 ). 3. We demonstrate strong monitoring performance across diverse simulated policy–benchmark settings (Section 5.2 ) and real-world manipulation tasks (Section 5.3 ), together with detailed analyses of the detector and predictor components (Section 5.4 ). 2 Related Work Runtime Failure Monitoring Existing runtime failure monitors estimate risk from different execution-time signals. Based on how these signals are processed to assess failure risk, existing approaches can be broadly grouped into four families. OOD-based methods detect deviations from successful or in-distribution behavior ( Burda et al., 2019 ; Wong et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Action-uncertainty methods use signals from generated actions or the action-generation process, including action resampling, diffusion objectives, and flow-matching dynamics ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Rao et al., 2026 ) . Supervised detectors learn failure scores from labeled executions using visual, temporal, or policy representations ( Farid et al., 2022 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . Foundation-model-based approaches use pretrained language or vision-language models for semantic failure detection and reasoning ( Sinha et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2025 ; Pacaud et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Hybrid methods combine multiple signals. FIPER ( Römer et al., 2025 ) combines observation novelty with action uncertainty, while SENTINEL ( Agia et al., 2025 ) combines action uncertainty with VLM-based progress monitoring. A separate line of predictive monitoring models future states under proposed actions. Liu et al. (2024) simulate future policy rollouts with latent dynamics. Concurrent works include Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which uses action-conditioned world-model features for failure detection, and ContactGuard ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which scores predicted post-contact latents with a failure probe. In comparison, ReAP first learns a failure-relevant representation space and models action consequences in this space to estimate future failure risk, considering both current visual signals and future action risks. Further comparisons are provided in Appendix A . Test-Time Action Evaluation. A growing body of work evaluates candidate actions proposed by robot policies before execution. Recent approaches use learned verifiers, reward models, history-aware verification, or model-internal confidence signals to score and select among multiple action proposals ( Kwok et al., 2025 ; Dai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) . These methods score candidate actions without explicitly predicting their future consequences. A complementary line of work predicts the consequences of candidate actions before evaluation. FOREWARN ( Wu et al., 2025 ) uses a latent world model to imagine candidate outcomes and aligns the predicted latent states with a VLM for consequence evaluation. DynaGuide ( Du and Song, 2025 ) predicts future latent states and uses their similarity to desired or undesired outcomes to guide action generation, while Do What You Say ( Wu et al., 2026 ) forward-simulates candidate action sequences and evaluates whether the predicted outcomes agree with the policy’s textual reasoning. Our method is most closely related to this predictive line, as we use this predictive capability as a runtime monitoring signal by evaluating the estimated representation in the failure-relevant space learned by the visual detector to assess risk before action execution. 3 Problem Setup We consider runtime failure monitoring for robotic manipulation policies. When queried at environment timestep t t , the deployed policy receives the visual observation O t O_{t} and proposes an action chunk A t π A_{t}^{\pi} of length H π H_{\pi} . The observation-based detector estimates current-state risk r t det r_{t}^{\mathrm{det}} , while the action-conditioned predictor estimates future risk r t + H | t pred r_{t+H|t}^{\mathrm{pred}} associated with executing the first H H actions of A t π A_{t}^{\pi} , denoted by A t = ( a t | t , … , a t + H − 1 | t ) A_{t}=(a_{t|t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1|t}) , where H H is the prediction horizon. Together, they support failure recognition from observed states and anticipation of risky action consequences before execution. The monitoring objective is to detect failed executions as early as possible while limiting false alarms on successful rollouts. Both models are trained on successful and failed rollouts collected from the policy, using only episode-level outcomes. For rollout i i of length T i T_{i} , the risk target is y i , t = 0 y_{i,t}=0 if the rollout succeeds and y i , t = t / ( T i − 1 ) y_{i,t}=t/(T_{i}-1) if it fails, where t ∈ { 0 , … , T i − 1 } t\in\{0,\ldots,T_{i}-1\} . This weak supervision avoids failure-onset annotation and assigns lower risk to early frames that may still appear nominal, with the target increasing to one at the end of a failed rollout. Figure 2: Overview of ReAP. Stage 1 learns an observation-based failure representation and detector. Stage 2 freezes the detector and learns an action-conditioned transition model that predicts future representations, which are evaluated by the same detector head. 4 Methods As shown in Figure 2 , our framework is trained in two stages. In Stage 1, an observation-only failure detector learns a failure-relevant visual representation using episode-level outcome supervision and maps it to a scalar risk score. In Stage 2, an action-conditioned transition model is trained in the latent space learned in Stage 1 to predict how the detector representation changes after executing a candidate action chunk. The predicted future representation is evaluated by the same frozen detector head, keeping the risk semantics of observed and predicted representations fixed. After training, thresholds for the detector and predictor are calibrated separately on held-out successful rollouts. 4.1 Observation-Only Failure Representation Learning Stage 1 learns a policy-external representation of failure from the current visual observation O t O_{t} , without accessing candidate actions or internal policy features. Each observation may contain one or more synchronized camera views. For each camera view, dense patch tokens are extracted using a frozen DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) backbone. The tokens are projected into a shared feature space and augmented with camera-specific and spatial positional embeddings. Tokens from all views are then concatenated to form the visual tokens of O t O_{t} . To compress the dense visual features into a failure-relevant representation, we use a Perceiver-style feature extractor ( Jaegle et al., 2021 ) with a fixed set of M M learnable latent queries. The latent queries aggregate visual information through cross-attention, using the projected DINOv2 patch tokens as keys and values. This produces a fixed set of M M detector latent tokens, denoted by L t L_{t} . We use M = 32 M=32 in all experiments. The detector latent tokens are first mean-pooled into a single vector that summarizes the current observation. A learned linear projection then maps this vector to the compact state representation z t z_{t} . Finally, the detector head maps z t z_{t} to the observation-level risk score r t det ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}\in[0,1] . During Stage 1 training, the DINOv2 backbone remains frozen, while the visual projection, Perceiver-style feature extractor, and detector head are optimized using failure supervision. To train the detector, we use a class-weighted binary cross-entropy loss over valid observation timesteps: ℒ det = − ∑ i ∑ t [ w + y i , t log r i , t det + w − ( 1 − y i , t ) log ( 1 − r i , t det ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=-\sum_{i}\sum_{t}\left[w_{+}y_{i,t}\log r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{det}}+w_{-}(1-y_{i,t})\log(1-r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{det}})\right], (1) where y i , t y_{i,t} is the risk target defined in Section 3 , and w + w_{+} and w − w_{-} compensate for class imbalance. 4.2 Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics in Failure Space Stage 2 models how a candidate action chunk changes the failure-relevant representation learned in Stage 1. Inspired by JEPA-style latent prediction ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) , we predict the representation of the future observation directly in the learned latent space rather than reconstructing the observation itself. The complete Stage 1 detector is frozen throughout this stage. Given the current compact representation z t z_{t} and the action proposal A t A_{t} available from the current policy query, each action is independently projected to the transition latent dimension and augmented with a learnable step embedding that encodes its position within the action chunk. The resulting action tokens serve as queries in stacked cross-attention blocks. To construct the keys and values, we apply linear projections independently to each token in L t L_{t} . The cross-attention blocks attend to these projected tokens and produce action-conditioned features over the prediction horizon. We mean-pool both the action tokens and the resulting action-conditioned features, and concatenate them with the current compact representation z t z_{t} . A residual transition MLP takes the concatenated features as input and predicts a latent update, which is added to the current representation z t z_{t} to obtain the future compact representation z ^ t + H | t \hat{z}_{t+H|t} . The predicted representation is passed through the frozen Stage 1 detector head to obtain the anticipated future risk r t + H | t pred r_{t+H|t}^{\mathrm{pred}} . During training, the actual future observation O t + H O_{t+H} is processed by the same frozen detector to obtain the target representation z t + H z_{t+H} . The transition model is trained to predict this future latent representation using an MSE objective together with future-risk supervision: ℒ pre = λ feat d ​ ‖ z ^ t + H | t − sg ⁡ ( z t + H ) ‖ 2 2 + λ risk ​ ℒ det future . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{feat}}}{d}\left\|\hat{z}_{t+H|t}-\operatorname{sg}(z_{t+H})\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{risk}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}^{\mathrm{future}}. (2) Here, d d denotes the compact state dimension and sg \operatorname{sg} stops gradients through the target representation. The future-risk loss ℒ det future \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}^{\mathrm{future}} follows Equation 1 using r t + H | t pred r_{t+H|t}^{\mathrm{pred}} . The two terms supervise future latent prediction and failure-risk estimation, respectively. We use λ feat = λ risk = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{feat}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{risk}}=1 by default. 4.3 Threshold Calibration Following prior work on time-dependent failure-score calibration ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , we calibrate monitoring thresholds using a held-out set of successful rollouts. Scores estimated may vary across execution phases even in successful rollouts, motivating thresholds that vary with time. To align score trajectories for calibration, we consider three temporal parameterizations. Absolute-time calibration indexes thresholds by the raw timestep t t . Normalized-time calibration represents each timestep by its relative progress within the trajectory. Staged-time calibration partitions normalized execution progress into a fixed number of stages and uses a shared threshold within each stage. For each temporal parameterization, we construct thresholds using either pointwise quantiles or a one-sided functional conformal band, resulting in six calibration variants. The detector and predictor are calibrated independently under the same protocol. For further details, refer to Appendix E . Let δ t det \delta_{t}^{\mathrm{det}} and δ t pred \delta_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}} denote their respective thresholds. At runtime, the monitor raises an alarm whenever either branch crosses its calibrated threshold: b t = [ r t det ≥ δ t det ] ∨ [ r t + H | t pred ≥ δ t pred ] . b_{t}=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[r_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}\geq\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{det}}\right]\lor\mathbbm{1}\!\left[r_{t+H|t}^{\mathrm{pred}}\geq\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}\right]. (3) 5 Experiments We evaluate ReAP in simulation and on real robots to answer three questions. (1) Does ReAP achieve a favorable balance between failure-detection accuracy, warning timeliness, and false alarms across diverse policies and tasks? (Section 5.2 and Appendix D.1 ) (2) Can ReAP maintain effective online monitoring on real robots while introducing low inference overhead? (Section 5.3 ) (3) What enables its monitoring performance, and how do failure-relevant representation learning and action-conditioned prediction contribute to the final monitor? (Section 5.4 and Appendix D.2 ) 5.1 Experiment Setup Baselines. We compare ReAP with representative runtime failure monitors from three categories. Action-uncertainty methods estimate failure risk from the policy’s action-generation process. STAC ( Agia et al., 2025 ) measures inconsistency across sampled actions, Diff-DAgger ( Lee et al., 2025 ) uses diffusion-model objectives as uncertainty signals, and ACCEL ( Rao et al., 2026 ) derives uncertainty from flow-matching trajectories. OOD-based methods identify failures from deviations relative to successful execution. We include RND ( Burda et al., 2019 ) and LogpZO ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , and additionally evaluate FIPER ( Römer et al., 2025 ) , which augments an observation-based OOD signal with action uncertainty. Classifier-based methods directly learn failure risk from successful and failed rollouts. We include SAFE-MLP and SAFE-LSTM ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , which operate on internal VLA representations extracted from the deployed policy. Evaluation Protocols. Following Römer et al. (2025) , we evaluate runtime monitoring with three complementary metrics, balanced time-weighted accuracy (bTWA), balanced accuracy (bACC), and normalized detection time (T-det). bACC measures failure-detection accuracy while accounting for false alarms on successful rollouts, with bACC = ( TPR + TNR ) / 2 \mathrm{bACC}=(\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2 . T-det measures warning timeliness as the mean normalized first-alarm time over all failed rollouts, with missed failures assigned a value of one.
